title: Decades of High Nitrogen Deposition Mainly Enhanced Eutrophication Rather Than Acidification of Dutch Forest Soils
content:
Abstract

In the last decades, forest in the Netherlands have been exposed to high levels nitrogen (N) deposition, which allows to assess the fate and impacts of N and evaluate the concept of N saturation in this large scale “experiment” and related soil acidification. This was done by repeating an inventory of the stocks of nitrogen, in combination with carbon (C), with the base cations calcium (Ca), magnesium (Mg) and potassium (K) as well as aluminum (Al) and of the pH of the organic layer and topsoil (0–30 cm) of 127 forested stands on sandy soils across the Netherlands in 1990 and in 2023. Results showed an average soil N accumulation of 31 (±3.2) kg N ha−1 yr−1 in combination with an average soil C accumulation of 427 (±79) kg C ha−1 yr−1, mainly in the organic layer. The stocks of all base cations together also increased in the organic layer, but it decreased in the mineral layer, being nearly constant for both layers. However, the pools of aluminum decreased in both layers, being the main buffer of ongoing soil acidification, thereby keeping the average pH-KCl near 3.5. The ongoing soil acidification has been relatively limited due to high N accumulation and limited nitrate leaching, with average C/N ratios decreasing from 26.2 to 23.8, indicating that reaching full N saturation near a C/N ratio of 20 may still take decades in large parts of the forest.
